summary: Rebecca prepares Jacob to receive the blessing Isaac intends for Esau, and Jacob approaches his father wearing Esau's clothes and goat skins. Isaac blesses Jacob with abundance and rule, then confirms the blessing when Esau returns; Esau's bitter appeal ends with a prediction of subordination and destruction and a threat against Jacob.
whyItMatters: The chapter makes the transfer of ancestral blessing irreversible while exposing the deception, grief, and threatened violence within the family. Its claim that heaven impaired Isaac's perception is part of Jubilees' presentation of Jacob's election.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: The aged Isaac's household, where food, clothing, touch, voice, and smell shape a disputed blessing.
context.literaryForm: Family narrative with extended dialogue, ancestral blessings, and an explicit explanation of heavenly involvement.

before.text: Rebecca has blessed Jacob after he promises to marry within her family. The next contest concerns the blessing Isaac plans to give Esau.

here.text: Watch how Rebecca's disguise succeeds despite Isaac's doubts, and how Esau responds when the blessing cannot be recovered.

after.text: Rebecca learns of Esau's threat and arranges Jacob's departure; Isaac sends him away with a further blessing.

outline.heading: Isaac requests a final meal
outline.note: Isaac sends Esau hunting before the blessing he believes must precede his death.

outline.heading: Rebecca prepares the substitution
outline.note: Jacob fears recognition and a curse; Rebecca accepts that risk and disguises him.

outline.heading: Isaac questions and blesses Jacob
outline.note: The narrator attributes Isaac’s failed recognition to heaven and records the blessing.

outline.heading: Esau discovers the loss
outline.note: Isaac confirms the blessing while Esau protests and weeps.

outline.heading: A dark future and a threat
outline.note: Isaac speaks of Esau’s subordination and destruction, and Esau plans to kill Jacob.

keyVerses.text: 'The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau,' and he discerned him not, because it was a dispensation from heaven to remove his power of perception and Isaac discerned not, for his hands were hairy as his brother Esau's, so that he blessed him.
keyVerses.why: The narrator explicitly attributes failed recognition to heaven, a claim that complicates the deception.

keyVerses.text: Be lord over thy brethren, And let thy mother's sons bow down to thee; And may all the blessings wherewith the Lord hath blessed me and blessed Abraham, my father; Be imparted to thee and to thy seed for ever: Cursed be he that curseth thee, And blessed be he that blesseth thee.'
keyVerses.why: Isaac transfers ancestral blessing and authority to Jacob and his descendants.

keyVerses.text: And it came to pass when Esau heard the words of his father Isaac that he cried with an exceeding great and bitter cry, and said unto his father: 'Bless me, (even) me also, father.'
keyVerses.why: Esau’s bitter cry gives the dispossessed brother an unmistakable voice in the scene.

questions.question: Why does Isaac ask Esau to hunt?
questions.answer: Isaac expects to die and wants the food he loves before blessing his elder son. The request establishes why Esau is absent and why a meal becomes the occasion for the substitution.

questions.question: What worries Jacob about Rebecca’s plan?
questions.answer: He worries that Isaac will recognize his voice or smooth skin and judge him an evildoer. Rebecca says the curse can fall on her and supplies clothing and goat skins to make the deception work.

questions.question: Does Jacob directly say that he is Esau?
questions.answer: In this version Jacob says that he is Isaac's son, including when Isaac explicitly asks whether he is Esau. Those words occur within a deliberate disguise, so their narrower wording does not remove the scene's deception.

questions.question: What does “dispensation from heaven” mean here?
questions.answer: The narrator uses the phrase to explain why Isaac fails to identify Jacob: heaven removes his power of perception. It is the story's theological explanation of the outcome, not an observable account of how blindness or recognition normally works.

questions.question: What does the blessing give Jacob?
questions.answer: Isaac promises agricultural abundance, the service of nations, and authority over his brothers. He also passes on the blessings received by himself and Abraham, extending them to Jacob's descendants.

questions.question: Why is Esau’s reaction more than sibling annoyance?
questions.answer: He believes both birthright and blessing have been taken from him, and he repeatedly begs his father for a blessing of his own. The narrative records bitter crying and tears before his anger turns toward murder.

questions.question: Does the prediction about Esau authorize hostility toward his descendants?
questions.answer: Isaac's speech predicts servitude, rebellion, and the destruction of Esau's line; its severity should be stated plainly. The passage is an ancestral judgment within the narrative and supplies no warrant for a reader to threaten a contemporary people.

glossary.def: A solemn ancestral pronouncement concerning prosperity, descendants, and authority, treated here as consequential and enduring.
The elder son’s claim that Esau says he has already lost, distinguished in his complaint from the blessing.
Deception: Isaac’s description of the way Jacob obtained the blessing.
